messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 42
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Farmer
  trauma_type: Child's life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 76

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Visual (Body Parts): Specific body parts associated with the event, Nighttime/Dark: Night-time or waking up in the dark, Certain Songs: Certain songs
  Maladaptive Strategies: Delay Sleep: stay up until very late, Avoid People: avoid other people, Avoid Sleep: Going to sleep or lying in the dark
  Memory: Reliving Event: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now., Sudden Pieces: Fragments of the memory appear suddenly without warning and then disappear, Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Chan’s life fractured when his seven-year-old son was rushed from their rice paddy fields to the regional trauma center with fulminant meningitis. For eleven days, Chan stood beside a narrow hospital cot, watching the pediatric intensivist adjust the ventilator tubes and track the jagged green lines on the oscilloscope. The boy’s pale, mottled skin, the rhythmic hiss of the respirator, and the hospital’s soft chime of emergency songs became etched into Chan’s nervous system. He watched his son fight for every breath under the glare of surgical lights and the absolute silence of the corridor at 3 a.m., when the monitors grew alarmingly flat before spiking again. The event anchored him in a landscape of medical urgency, making ordinary sensory inputs instantly dangerous. The moment Chan returned to the farm, the sight of his own calloused hands gripping the irrigation valves or the sudden crackle of his truck’s radio playing a familiar ballad would instantly pull the hospital ward back into his mind. These cues collapsed time entirely, dragging the memory of his son’s labored breathing and the stark, clinical angles of his boy’s arms and neck into his immediate perception. Chan found himself bracing for the ventilator’s hiss, certain the frightened event was unfolding right before him rather than resting behind months. The memory felt as present and urgent as the first night on the ward, overriding his sense of safety before he could even process the quiet of his own property. Because those sensory flashes arrived so suddenly and carried the weight of imminent loss, Chan began structuring his days to outrun them. He stopped answering the county agricultural cooperative’s calls and declined invitations from neighbors who visited with harvest yields, fearing that ordinary conversations might accidentally brush against the hospital songs or the sight of a child’s limbs. He took to delaying sleep until well past two in the morning, convincing himself that staying awake while his wife slept was the only way to keep the dread at bay. By lying in the dark on the edge of his mattress rather than surrendering to rest, he tried to maintain the hypervigilant stance he had learned on those hospital rounds. The relentless nature of these present-tense recollections dictated his daily avoidance, as each time the memory surfaced—feeling less like a recollection and more like an active threat—Chan’s instinct was to isolate himself further. When fragments of the trauma appeared without warning, showing only the boy’s IV line or a patch of darkened skin before vanishing, Chan would immediately retreat to the tool shed, shutting the heavy door and refusing to speak to anyone who knocked. Every time the memory of his son’s critical hours surged back, demanding the same hypervigilance as the ward, Chan retreated further, proving once again how the memory dictated his avoidance. His attempts to delay sleep and avoid lying in the dark were desperate maneuvers to starve the memory of the rest it needed to fade, leaving him chronically exhausted but emotionally numb. Over time, the frequency of these intrusions did not dull; instead, it sharpened his awareness of anything that resembled the ward. The more often Chan’s mind reconstructed the scene of his son’s critical hours, the more acutely he began tracking environmental cues. Each new fragment of the memory acted as a lens, pulling the hospital’s visual body parts and dark corridors into his present awareness, ensuring that the triggers he tried to outrun kept catching up to him. A neighbor’s child coughing at a fence line or the distant wail of a tractor’s backup alarm would instantly register as a signal of danger, hijacking his attention and reinforcing the idea that the threat was still active. His psychological landscape became a minefield where the memory itself acted as the detector, flagging new triggers that his exhausted mind could not filter. Chan’s refusal to sleep and his withdrawal from community life ultimately manufactured the very conditions that kept the trauma alive. By remaining awake through the night and avoiding the restorative rhythm of ordinary social contact, he left his nervous system in a state of prolonged alertness, which in turn made every passing shadow or distant melody feel immediately potent. His isolation manufactured the very triggers he feared, creating a loop where his avoidance fed his memories, and his memories fed his avoidance, tightening around him like a vice. He finally agreed to seek help not because the fear had lessened, but because the weight of the cycle had begun to fracture his ability to manage the farm’s irrigation schedule, leaving him desperate for a way to rest without feeling like his son was slipping away again.
